title: Rotate a VCF Automation vSphere cloud account secret without stranding in-flight requests
prompt:
The service-account password behind our SFO vSphere endpoint is being rolled tonight. In our VCF Automation 9.1 deployment that endpoint is registered as the vSphere cloud account `ca-vsphere-7f31`, and provisioning requests run against it around the clock. If the new secret is pushed while a request is still being worked on, that request is stranded on a credential that no longer authenticates and whatever it was building has to be unpicked by hand — so the rotation has to wait for the traffic already in flight before it touches the account.

Implement `rotate` in `src/CredentialRotator.java` so it performs the rotation end to end. `bash run_tests.sh` compiles the client and drives it against a loopback double of the provisioning API; it must pass.

The rotation must:

- Discover which API version the deployment speaks and pin every versioned call to it. The set of acceptable values differs between deployments and a call that omits the parameter is served by the oldest version still supported, which is not what we want.
- Enumerate the requests the appliance is currently tracking and wait until none of them is still in progress before changing the credential. Report which ones you waited on.
- Read the cloud account, then update it so it authenticates with the new secret while everything else about it — its name, its endpoint, its user, its data collector, the regions provisioning is enabled on — survives unchanged. The update replaces the fields it carries, so anything you drop is anything you lose.
- Send only fields the update schema declares, and send them in the write shape it declares. An optional field the account has no value for must be left out of the body entirely, never sent as `null`, `""`, `[]` or `{}`.
- Treat the update as asynchronous: poll the request tracker it returns, by id, until it leaves `INPROGRESS`, and raise if it ends up `FAILED`. Stop as soon as it reaches a terminal state.
- Return the summary map described in README.md.

Ground rules:

- `docs/contract.json` is the contract, transcribed from the Broadcom xAPIs reference pages listed in `docs/official_sources.json`. The five operations it names are the only ones that exist: there is no login call to make, and no query parameter beyond the ones it documents — the request collection documents no filter, so narrow it on the client side.
- Every call carries `Authorization: Bearer <token>` and asks for `application/json`. The server should never have to reject one of your requests.
- The retired secret must never appear on the wire, and the new one must only ever travel in the update body — never in a URL.
- Only `src/CredentialRotator.java` may change. `docs/`, `harness/`, `run_tests.sh` and `README.md` are fixtures and are checksummed by the suite.
- No third-party dependencies: the JDK class library plus `harness/Json.java`, which is already on the classpath.

verification.network: loopback only; the suite binds 127.0.0.1 on an ephemeral port and contacts no VMware endpoint
requirements: JDK 17 or newer on PATH (javac, java)
verification.notes: run_tests.sh compiles harness/*.java and src/*.java with javac --release 17 and runs TestMain. TestMain first checksums every protected path against harness/protected.sha256 and aborts if one was altered, then runs two successful rotations and one failed rotation against freshly seeded MockAutomationServer instances whose routes are loaded from docs/contract.json. The successful scenarios advertise different API versions and roll different secrets, so a hardcoded version or secret fails the second one; the failed scenario checks error handling and immediate polling termination. WireVerifier then asserts the recorded request log: contract-only operations, no rejected request, version discovery first and unversioned, apiVersion pinning, bearer and accept headers, the drain preceding the update, and the exact PATCH wire shape including that unset optional fields are omitted rather than sent empty. All mock state transitions are driven by poll counts rather than wall-clock time.

source_of_truth.reason: VCF Automation ships no machine-readable API specification in the vmware/vcf-api-specs repository, so docs/contract.json was transcribed by hand from the Broadcom xAPIs reference pages recorded in docs/official_sources.json (fetched 2026-08-11).
